prompt:
You read transcripts of Bitcoin videos. For each EXCERPT below, the sentences inside <selected> are a clip
that may be shown on its own. Use the whole excerpt (what comes before and after) to judge the selected words. You do
not know how the clip will be used.

<excerpt label="1eff6e75d00b8de8cf95" channel="Simply Bitcoin" video_title="Bitcoin Just Puked to $62K. Is a COVID-Level Crash Coming Next?" published="2026-11-16T22:00" show_date="2026-11-17">60. In the summer, we hit 58 and then went dead and flat for two months while everyone waited for 45. Then when almost nobody believed it, Bitcoin ripped to 87,000 in one of the biggest short squeezes in its history. And everyone started saying the bear market was over, me included. And now here we are, back at 62. Every time the crowd got sure about a direction, this market did the opposite. The bears who were sure we would hit 45 got squeezed, and the bulls who were sure of 100 just got flushed. That's what Max Payne looks like. The market moves in whatever way hurts the most people, and Bitcoin bear markets have always worked like that. This one has reiterated what I found out in my first cycle. This market is basically impossible to predict. So if I had to guess at the cruelest path from here, it would be one more sweep of the lows to shake out the last of the longs, and then a violent move back up towards $90,000 that wipes out everyone betting against it. Now that's just a thought experiment and I definitely wouldn't trade it, but that's my version of Max Payne. A friend of mine asked over the weekend if he should just sell his Bitcoin now. His thinking was that since Trump lost the midterms, maybe Bitcoin has just lost the wind in its sales. I told him the thesis has not changed. And he's not alone in asking, and I don't blame him. Jeff Swanson put it well today. You can't explain Bitcoin to someone who doesn't understand money in the first place. A lot of people bought Bitcoin because the price was going up, and nobody ever told them why it exists. So when the price falls, they've got nothing to hold on to. So let's answer my friend properly. <selected>Bitcoin was never riding on a president. The strategic Bitcoin Reserve still hasn't bought a single coin. And Bitcoin grew into a trillion dollar asset under governments that ignored it or outright fought against it. The thesis is centered around money. A government that owes $40 trillion has to keep making its money worth less, no matter who wins an election.</selected> election. And Bitcoin is the one form of money that nobody can make more of. That was true at $126,000, and it's true at $62,000. Nothing about the Bitcoin thesis changed this weekend. And you can see it in the data. If you strip out the noise and look at the average price the whole network paid for its coins smoothed out over four years, it sits around $38,000 today. And it's gone up every single year on this chart. So should you sell your Bitcoin before it gets worse? If you understand what you own, I don't see a single reason to. And if you don't understand it yet, this is the time to learn before you make a decision you can't take back. This weekend sorted people by why they own Bitcoin. The ones who owned a price sold. And the ones who owned the reason didn't move. And if a bigger crash comes next, it'll sort all of us again. Bitcoin can protect your savings. but your piece has to come from somewhere deeper than a price. Bitcoin is living up to its reputation. It keeps producing a block every 10 minutes</excerpt>

For each excerpt answer:
- "speaker_changes_inside": does the speaker change inside the selected words? "yes" / "no" / "uncertain"
- "view": whose view the selected words express: "own_sincere" (the speaker's own sincere assertion), "attributed"
  (someone else's view, quoted or reported), "hypothetical", "conditional" (true only under a condition), "sarcastic",
  "question", "reading_aloud" (reading a post or article), "ad_read", "joke", or "uncertain"
- "referents": every pronoun or pointing word in the selected words (it, they, this, that, he, she, today, here...)
  that points at something specific, with what it refers to; "inside": true if the selected words themselves give
  its antecedent or the predicate that completes it (an ellipsis completed by an earlier selected sentence: "It's not
  Bitcoin that's getting hacked. It's other intermediaries." = other intermediaries are getting hacked), or it points
  only at a general topic the clip presupposes; "inside": false if a listener needs the words before or after the
  selection; "changes_assertion": "yes" if resolving it differently would change WHAT THE SPEAKER ASSERTS, "no" if
  not, "uncertain". Leave out words that point at nothing outside: a dummy "it" ("it's raining", "it's not X that
  ...", where X is in the selection), and a generic "we" / "you" / "they" meaning people in general
- "conditions": any condition or time frame that governs the selected words, and whether it is INSIDE them
- "retraction": "none", or what the speaker later in the excerpt WITHDRAWS, REVERSES, CORRECTS or MATERIALLY LIMITS
  about the selected words ("actually I misspoke", "that said, I don't believe that", "but that only holds if ...").
  A later elaboration or warning that is CONSISTENT with a condition already stated inside the selected words is not
  a retraction ("none"); it would be one if the selected words had dropped that condition
- "time_ok": "yes" if every time word in the selected words (today, now, this week, just, recently, a "current"
  price) still holds on the show date given when the video was published (both on the excerpt), or there is none;
  "no" if it is stale; "uncertain"
- "proposition": in one sentence, what the speaker asserts in the selected words, read in context
- "certainty": "certain", "likely", "possible", "speculative" or "uncertain"
- "speaker_is": "host" if the excerpt shows that the speaker of the selected words is the channel's own host,
  "guest" if it shows a guest or another person speaking them, "uncertain" otherwise; "speaker_evidence": the exact
  words of the excerpt that show it (copied exactly, e.g. the host's own "welcome back to my channel"), or ""
